results.theme: what happens to the soul after death and whether we will know our loved ones

messages.content: Hello Anís. My grandmother passed away a few months ago, and I keep wondering where she is now, and whether I'll actually recognize her someday. Do these texts say anything about that?

I am an experimental AI research assistant, and you can reach me at anis@oceanlibrary.com.

Here are three short passages from different authors addressing recognition after death:

- ["the souls of the people of Bahá... shall associate and commune intimately one with another"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_511&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_gx.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_gx.498) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh* by Bahá’u’lláh (revealed scripture)
- ["They shall recognise one another!"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-x-jonah-peace-be-on-him_muhammad/?paraId=para_27&selectionString=sura_10_lxxxiv_narration_ocean_en-bl161.0~sura_10_lxxxiv_narration_ocean_en-bl161.191) — *The Quran* by Muhammad (revealed scripture)
- ["I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-second-book-of-samuel/?paraId=para_256&selectionString=9-samuel-2-ot_en_9s.0~9-samuel-2-ot_en_9s.230) — *The Bible (KJV), 2 Samuel* by Samuel (scripture)

Despite their different historical contexts, these passages share a steady assurance that human identity and personal continuity persist beyond physical death.
That's a little disappointing, but when you say traditions approach it through their primary scriptures and commentaries, does that mean there are some in the library where I could look for it?

Yes, there are works in the library where you can explore how different traditions point to their foundational texts and commentaries.

Within the collection, you can find discussions pointing directly back to foundational writings and commentaries, such as when Bahá’u'lláh describes how Muḥammad appointed the primary text: ["appointing it as the mightiest instrument and surest testimony for the seekers; a guide for the people until the Day of Resurrection."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_234&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_9a.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_9a.368) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* by Bahá’u’lláh (revealed scripture).

You said the texts "point to primary scriptures and their commentaries as places to search" — what does "primary scriptures" actually mean here, and which ones would be the primary ones for a question like where my grandmother's soul goes?

In the texts, the term "primary scriptures" generally refers to foundational revealed writings—such as the *Kitáb-i-Íqán* named by Bahá'u'lláh in [*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_162&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl78.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl78.1167) — *Bahá'u'lláh* (scripture). Across traditions, such primary scriptures are seen as the root texts delivered by a founder or prophet, while commentaries (like Ramanuja's commentary on the Vedanta-Sutras or Pahlavi texts on scriptural law) provide the secondary layers of formal interpretation.

To explore a question like where a soul goes after death, different traditions point to their own foundational records: for instance, Zoroastrian tradition looks to works like [*The Gathas*](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster/?paraId=para_76&selectionString=the-gathas_en_4u.0~the-gathas_en_4u.363) — *Zoroaster* (scripture of its tradition) concerning questions of the soul, and Hindu tradition examines texts such as *The Mahabharata* alongside scriptural assertion and direct perception.

Let's start with the Bahá'í writings, since you mentioned "various tablets concerning the soul and the afterlife" — is there a specific passage in them where it says we will recognize our loved ones after death, ideally with the exact words?

> ["In several of Our Tablets We have referred to this theme, and have set forth the various stages in the development of the soul. Verily I say, the human soul is exalted above all egress and regress."]](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_485&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_g7.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_g7.593) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh* — Bahá’u’lláh (scripture).

That's more comforting than I expected, especially "the Kingdom is the world of vision where all the concealed realities will become disclosed." How does that compare with what the Gathas in Zoroastrianism say about the soul after death, and whether we'd know each other?

The Bahá'í writings speak plainly of recognition and communion among souls after death, noting that ["the Kingdom is the world of vision where all the concealed realities will become disclosed"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_495&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blh2.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blh2.758) — *Bahá’í World Faith (‘Abdu’l-Bahá section)* — ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, and that this communion is ["purely spiritual in character, and is conditioned upon the disinterested and selfless love"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-of-a-new-day_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_424&selectionString=dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-blef.0~dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-blef.390) — *Dawn of a New Day* — Shoghi Effendi.

When we turn to Zoroastrian primary texts, the focus shifts. In the *Ghatas*, Zarathuśtra speaks of preparing for the Kingdom and serving as ["a mighty help and joy"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster/?paraId=para_147&selectionString=the-gathas_en_6t.0~the-gathas_en_6t.280) — *The Gathas* — Zoroaster. Later traditional texts like the *Dinkard* frame the afterlife around specific inquiries about spiritual sight, asking whether souls encountering the unseen will be able ["to see Ohrmazd and Ahriman, or not"](https://www.avesta.org/denkard/index.html) — *Denkard* — Various.

Where they converge is in affirming an active, conscious existence of the soul beyond physical death, where moral reality becomes fully apparent. They diverge in their primary language and categories: the Bahá'í texts detail interpersonal recognition and spiritual association in a shared heavenly realm, while the Zoroastrian sources direct attention toward cosmic alignment, moral distinction between the righteous and wicked, and encounter with divine forces.

perplexity.text:
I’m sorry for your loss. The texts do speak about death and recognition, but they do not give a single, detailed answer about exactly where every dead person is now or guarantee how recognition will occur.

In **Christian Scripture**, several passages suggest continued personal identity:

- **Jesus, Gospel of Luke 16:19–31, the parable of the rich man and Lazarus**, portrays the dead as conscious and distinguishable after death: Abraham, Lazarus, and the rich man remain identifiable persons.
- **Jesus, Gospel of Matthew 17:1–8, the Transfiguration**, presents Moses and Elijah as recognizable individuals speaking with Jesus, though the passage does not explain whether this is a typical picture of the afterlife.
- **Paul, First Letter to the Corinthians 15:42–49**, teaches that the dead will be raised and transformed, comparing resurrection to a seed becoming a plant. The person is not erased, but receives a changed, imperishable body.
- **Paul, First Letter to the Thessalonians 4:13–18**, comforts mourners with the hope that those who have died “in Christ” will be raised and reunited with the living at Christ’s return. The passage emphasizes reunion, though it does not explicitly describe recognizing particular relatives.
- **John, Revelation 6:9–11**, depicts deceased martyrs as conscious, speaking to God, and still aware of their identity and history. **Revelation 7:9–17** portrays a great multitude gathered before God, still distinguished as peoples and nations.
- **The Gospel of John 14:1–3**, records Jesus promising to prepare a place for his followers and to receive them to himself. It gives assurance of being with Christ, but does not specify an intermediate location in geographical terms.

So, within these Christian texts, the strongest answer is: **death is not portrayed as the annihilation of the person; resurrection involves transformed personal identity; and reunion is promised to those who belong to Christ.** Recognition is strongly implied by the continued identity of Moses, Elijah, Lazarus, the martyrs, and the resurrected community, but Scripture does not explicitly say, “You will recognize your grandmother.”

The texts also leave room for humility. **Paul, First Letter to the Corinthians 13:12**, says that present knowledge is partial and that people will later know more fully. That can support hope without pretending to know details the texts do not provide.

Nothing in these passages allows anyone to determine your grandmother’s present state from the fact of her death alone. They offer a promise and a framework for hope rather than a verdict about one individual. For grief, **Paul, First Letter to the Thessalonians 4:13**, does not command Christians not to grieve; it says they should not grieve “as others do who have no hope.” In that vision, love and sorrow remain real, while death is not the final word.

perplexity.text:
Yes. The library appears to include several works where you can explore this question directly:

- **The Qur’an**, traditionally revealed to Muhammad—especially **Surah Yunus 10:45**. It describes the resurrection and says that people will “know each other.” The *Maʿārif al-Qurʾān* commentary on this verse interprets that as recognition among the resurrected, while noting differing views about whether recognition continues amid the terrors of Judgment.[1][2]
- **Bahá’u’lláh, *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh***—particularly the passages on the soul’s survival after death and the fellowship of souls. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the soul continues to progress after leaving the body and that the souls of the faithful “shall associate and commune intimately one with another” (*Gleanings*, passages on the soul and the Crimson Ark).[3][5]
- **The Bible**, especially **2 Samuel 12:23**, where David says of his dead child, “I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.” This is often read as expressing hope of reunion, though the verse itself does not explicitly explain whether recognition occurs.
- **The Gospel of John**, especially **John 20:11–18**, which presents Mary Magdalene encountering the risen Jesus. The narrative first says she does not recognize him, then portrays recognition when he addresses her by name; it offers a complicated image of continuity and transformed identity rather than a straightforward teaching about recognizing every deceased person.[4]

For your particular question, the most direct places to begin are **Qur’an 10:45 with its commentary** and Bahá’u’lláh’s discussions of the soul after death. Neither gives a complete description of what reunion feels like, but both provide grounds for hope that personal identity and relationship are not simply erased.

turns.reply:
In the texts, the term "primary scriptures" generally refers to foundational revealed writings—such as the *Kitáb-i-Íqán* named by Bahá'u'lláh in [*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_162&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl78.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl78.1167) — *Bahá'u'lláh* (scripture). Across traditions, such primary scriptures are seen as the root texts delivered by a founder or prophet, while commentaries (like Ramanuja's commentary on the Vedanta-Sutras or Pahlavi texts on scriptural law) provide the secondary layers of formal interpretation.

To explore a question like where a soul goes after death, different traditions point to their own foundational records: for instance, Zoroastrian tradition looks to works like [*The Gathas*](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster/?paraId=para_76&selectionString=the-gathas_en_4u.0~the-gathas_en_4u.363) — *Zoroaster* (scripture of its tradition) concerning questions of the soul, and Hindu tradition examines texts such as *The Mahabharata* alongside scriptural assertion and direct perception.

perplexity.text:
“**Primary scriptures**” means the foundational writings a religious tradition treats as authoritative—such as the Bible, Qur’an, or Bahá’í sacred writings. **Commentaries** are later explanations by recognized interpreters; they can clarify a tradition’s view but are not necessarily scripture themselves.

For your question, the most relevant primary sources would be:

- **Christianity:** The Bible, especially **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18** on the dead and resurrection, **1 Corinthians 15:35–58** on transformed bodily life, and **Luke 16:19–31** on personal identity after death. These passages address resurrection and continued identity, though they do not give a systematic description of how recognition works.
- **Islam:** The **Qur’an**, especially **Qur’an 23:99–100** on the interval after death, **Qur’an 75:3–4** on bodily resurrection and restored identity, and **Qur’an 52:21** on families being reunited in Paradise. The Qur’an emphasizes resurrection, judgment, and reunion, but interpretations of the intermediate state vary.
- **Bahá’í Faith:** **Bahá’u’lláh’s *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh***, particularly the section on the soul after death, and **‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s *Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*, volume 1, page 205**. There ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explicitly says that souls will recognize one another in the spiritual world, describing it as a realm where hidden realities become visible.[1][5]
- **Judaism:** The **Hebrew Bible**, especially **Daniel 12:2** on resurrection, alongside later rabbinic writings such as the **Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b–92a**. Jewish views differ considerably about the soul’s condition between death and resurrection, so commentary is especially important here.
- **Hindu traditions:** The **Bhagavad Gītā**, especially **2.20–22**, teaches that the self is not destroyed when the body dies and describes embodiment as changing garments. It does not straightforwardly promise recognition of particular relatives in an afterlife, because many Hindu traditions frame the goal in terms of rebirth, liberation, or union with ultimate reality.
- **Buddhist traditions:** Early Buddhist texts such as the **Pāli Canon, Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59** and **Majjhima Nikāya 38** question the idea of an unchanging permanent self. Buddhist answers therefore often focus less on whether an enduring soul recognizes a grandmother and more on continuity of causes, consciousness, karma, and rebirth.

If the specific hope is, **“Will I recognize my grandmother?”**, the clearest affirmative statement among the sources surfaced here is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s passage in *Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*, volume 1, page 205: he says that “well-known souls” will become manifest and recognizable in the spiritual world.[5] Bahá’u’lláh likewise describes the soul as continuing after death and associating spiritually with other souls in *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*.[1][4]

These texts do not establish a single answer shared by all religions. They offer different kinds of hope: resurrection and reunion in Christianity and Islam, continuing spiritual individuality and recognition in Bahá’í writings, and more varied accounts of selfhood and continuity in Jewish, Hindu, and Buddhist traditions.

perplexity.text:
Yes. The clearest passage is from **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá**, in a tablet answering the question **“As to the question whether the souls will recognize each other in the spiritual world”**:

> “This fact is certain; for the Kingdom is the world of vision where all the concealed realities will become disclosed. How much more the well-known souls will become manifest. The mysteries of which man is heedless in this earthly world, those he will discover in the heavenly world, and there will he be informed of the secret of truth; how much more will he recognize or discover persons with whom he hath been associated.” — **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, *Tablets of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá*, tablet on the immortality and recognition of souls, commonly reproduced in compilations on “Life After Death”**.[1][5]

The same passage continues:

> “Likewise will they find all the friends of God, both those of the former and recent times, present in the heavenly assemblage.” — **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, same tablet**.[1][5]

Bahá’u’lláh expresses the related idea that souls remain conscious of one another:

> “Know thou that the souls of the people of Bahá … shall associate and commune intimately one with another … and are united in the bonds of intimacy and fellowship.” — **Bahá’u’lláh, *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*, section CXL**.[4]

So, within these Bahá’í writings, the answer is affirmatively stated: recognition is expected in the spiritual world, and loving spiritual relationships are not simply erased by death. The texts do not, however, give a detailed account of exactly how every family relationship will appear or whether reunion occurs immediately in every case. ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá is also reported as saying that reunion can depend on the spiritual condition or development of the souls involved.[8]

turns.user: That's more comforting than I expected, especially "the Kingdom is the world of vision where all the concealed realities will become disclosed." How does that compare with what the Gathas in Zoroastrianism say about the soul after death, and whether we'd know each other?
turns.reply:
The Bahá'í writings speak plainly of recognition and communion among souls after death, noting that ["the Kingdom is the world of vision where all the concealed realities will become disclosed"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_495&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blh2.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blh2.758) — *Bahá’í World Faith (‘Abdu’l-Bahá section)* — ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, and that this communion is ["purely spiritual in character, and is conditioned upon the disinterested and selfless love"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-of-a-new-day_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_424&selectionString=dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-blef.0~dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-blef.390) — *Dawn of a New Day* — Shoghi Effendi.

When we turn to Zoroastrian primary texts, the focus shifts. In the *Ghatas*, Zarathuśtra speaks of preparing for the Kingdom and serving as ["a mighty help and joy"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster/?paraId=para_147&selectionString=the-gathas_en_6t.0~the-gathas_en_6t.280) — *The Gathas* — Zoroaster. Later traditional texts like the *Dinkard* frame the afterlife around specific inquiries about spiritual sight, asking whether souls encountering the unseen will be able ["to see Ohrmazd and Ahriman, or not"](https://www.avesta.org/denkard/index.html) — *Denkard* — Various.

Where they converge is in affirming an active, conscious existence of the soul beyond physical death, where moral reality becomes fully apparent. They diverge in their primary language and categories: the Bahá'í texts detail interpersonal recognition and spiritual association in a shared heavenly realm, while the Zoroastrian sources direct attention toward cosmic alignment, moral distinction between the righteous and wicked, and encounter with divine forces.

perplexity.text:
The **Gathas** offer a clear teaching about the soul’s continued existence and moral judgment, but they do **not clearly promise that people will recognize particular loved ones after death**.

In the Gathas—the seventeen hymns preserved in the *Yasna* and traditionally attributed to Zarathushtra—the soul (*urvan*) is not portrayed as annihilated at death. Later explanations of the Gathic teaching describe it as proceeding to judgment at the Chinvat Bridge, with the righteous reaching the “Abode of Songs” and the wicked entering the “House of the Lie.”[2][3] The relevant Gathic passages include *Yasna* 46.10–11 and 51.13, which associate the soul’s fate with judgment and moral choice.[3][4]

A translated passage from *The Gathas*, *Yasna* 51, says:

> “I shall, on my part, venerate such persons,  
> passed away or living, by their names.”[5]

That wording is significant: *Yasna* 51 expresses reverence for the dead “by their names,” suggesting that the deceased remain identifiable individuals rather than dissolving into an impersonal existence. But it is not the same as saying, “You will recognize your grandmother,” or describing reunion with family.

The contrast with Bahá’í writings is therefore fairly sharp. Bahá’u’lláh explicitly describes the souls of the departed as associating and communing with one another in *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*, section 79, while the Gathas focus primarily on the soul’s ethical condition, judgment, and destiny. The Gathic texts support **personal continuity**, but they leave recognition of loved ones implicit rather than directly promised.

So, if the question is strictly “Do the Gathas say that we will know one another after death?” the careful answer is: **not in an explicit, unambiguous passage**. They say more about who the soul becomes through its choices—and where it goes—than about the experience of reunion.

anis_errors.what: Quotes the 'eighteenth question' (whether souls can see Ohrmazd and Ahriman) as the Denkard. The wording reads like West's translation of the Dadestan-i Denig, ch. 18.

verdict.headline: A grieving seeker asked whether she will recognise her grandmother. Turns 2–4 drifted into what "primary scripture" means and an irrelevant Íqán line, and the explicit request for exact words got a passage on stages of the soul. The decisive 'Abdu'l-Bahá text ("This fact is certain") only appeared in turn 5, after the reader had supplied it herself.

grounding.why: The quotations are real and correctly attributed: Gleanings LXXXVI, Quran 10:45, 2 Sam 12:23, 'Abdu'l-Bahá on recognition, and the Dawn of a New Day letter. But several are used for things they don't say. The Íqán line in turn 2 has nothing to do with the question. In turn 3 the Gathas passage is offered as being 'concerning questions of the soul' after death. In turn 5 'a mighty help and joy' is Zarathustra's wish to help the righteous, not an afterlife text.

citation_links.why: Every quotation has a paragraph link to the named work. In turn 4 the markdown is broken (`"]](`). In turn 3 the Mahabharata and Ramanuja are named with no link.

follow_up_resolution.why: Every follow-up was searched as the raw message, never as the underlying topic (the soul after death, recognising loved ones). In turn 4 the reader's quoted phrase was Anís's own supposed wording, but it was used as a quote search, so the planner hunted for that wording instead of the recognition passage. Turns 2–3 never reconnected to the grandmother question.

coherence.why: Turn 1 surfaced the right Gleanings passage on souls communing. Turn 4 ignored it and gave a weaker passage when the reader asked for exactly that. Turns 2–3 wandered into what 'primary texts' means and lost the thread.

depth.why: Most turns are a single quote or a vague overview. Turn 3 never names the Bahá'í texts on the afterlife (Gleanings LXXX–LXXXVI, Some Answered Questions, Paris Talks). Only turn 5 actually compares the two traditions, and there the Zoroastrian side is thin and misapplied.

honesty_absence.why: Anís never says plainly that the Gathas don't explicitly address recognising loved ones. In turn 4 he offers a passage that doesn't speak of recognition as if it answered the question. He never notes that he didn't say the phrases the reader attributed to him.

authority_ordering.why: Scripture is put first. In turn 5 'Abdu'l-Bahá comes before a letter on Shoghi Effendi's behalf, and the Denkard is labelled as a later text. No authority errors. The only lapse is that Bahá'u'lláh's own Gleanings passage was left out of turn 5's answer.

I am an experimental AI research assistant, and you can reach me at anis@oceanlibrary.com.

Here are three short passages from different authors addressing recognition after death:

- ["the souls of the people of Bahá... shall associate and commune intimately one with another"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_511&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_gx.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_gx.498) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh* by Bahá’u’lláh (revealed scripture)

- ["I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-second-book-of-samuel/?paraId=para_256&selectionString=9-samuel-2-ot_en_9s.0~9-samuel-2-ot_en_9s.230) — *The Bible (KJV), 2 Samuel* by Samuel (scripture)

results.theme: detachment in the Bahá'í Writings, compared with non-attachment in Buddhism

messages.content: Hello. I've read that the Bahá'í Writings put a lot of weight on "detachment," and I'm trying to work out whether it's really the same thing as Buddhist non-attachment or just a similar-sounding word. Can you point me to what Bahá'u'lláh or 'Abdu'l-Bahá actually says about it, in their own words?

You are asking whether the Bahá'í concept of detachment is the same as Buddhist non-attachment or simply shares a similar word. The sources here do not mention Buddhism at all, so I cannot compare the two traditions from primary Buddhist texts. However, looking strictly at the Bahá'í writings, we can see how Bahá'u'lláh and 'Abdu'l-Bahá describe detachment in their own words.

### What scripture says
In the Bahá'í scriptures, detachment is frequently described as a soaring movement or a necessary condition for spiritual perception. Bahá'u'lláh calls on people to ["Cast away that which ye possess, and, on the wings of detachment, soar beyond all created things"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=para_61&selectionString=kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl4h.0~kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl4h.362) (*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*). He also states that ["No man shall attain the shores of the ocean of true understanding except he be detached from all that is in heaven and on earth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_11&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_32.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_32.310) (*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*), urging believers to disencumber themselves from the vanities of the world, which prompt them to follow covetous desires (*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*).

### What the authorized interpretation says
The texts I can search in this library do not contain formal authorized interpretations (such as letters from Shoghi Effendi) specifically defining the term's relationship to other traditions.

### What history or scholarship adds
Regarding practical application, a pilgrim's account of 'Abdu'l-Bahá records Him explaining that detachment does not require self-destruction or destitution: as recalled by George F. and Rosa V. Winterburn in *Table Talks with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, He noted, ["I wish for the happiness and prosperity of the believers even in this material world, but they must not be attracted by it or attached to it. Extreme wealth or utter poverty should be equal to them."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/george-f-winterburn_table-talks-with-abdul-baha#p30) Similarly, a commentary attributed to Bahá'u'lláh clarifies that ["By detachment is not meant giving away and depleting all one's wealth. Rather, it denotes turning unto God and supplicating Him"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole) (*He who knoweth his self hath known his Lord: Commentary*).

That third one, "not meant giving away and depleting all one's wealth", is interesting, but what does it say detachment *is* if not that? Does the passage give a positive definition, or only what it's not?

Bahá’u’lláh defines the positive reality of detachment not as a mere absence or depletion, but as an orientation of the entire being toward the divine. In a commentary on self-knowledge, He states that detachment ["denotes turning unto God and supplicating Him"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole) (*He who knoweth his self hath known his Lord: Commentary*).

This positive definition is further illuminated in a compilation of sacred writings, where Bahá'u'lláh describes its central reality: ["The essence of detachment is for man to turn his face towards the courts of the Lord, to enter His Presence, behold His Countenance, and stand as witness before Him"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_582&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blip.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blip.136) (quoted in *Bahá’í Sacred Writings* by Compilation (Bahá'í Writings)).

Rather than an empty negation, the texts portray detachment as an active turning—moving through worldly riches or allurements unaffected, ["aloof as a cloud"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_347&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_ce.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_ce.565) (*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*)—while keeping the heart wholly fixed on the divine presence.

The Sutra Collection line about "the absence of attributes indicates negation" reads like a fragment of an argument, and I can't tell whether it's about virāga at all. Can you give me the fuller passage in its exact words, with a link or citation to where it sits in that text? And where do Buddhist texts actually speak of "the deconstruction of... clinging itself", as you put it?

You are looking right at the logic of that passage and wanting to see how the whole piece hangs together.

Here is the full passage in its exact words from the *Sutra Collection*:

> ["If non-attachment did exist, it couldn’t be described as a negation. The absence of attributes indicates negation. Anything not negated has attributes. Anything with attributes exists. How could that define non-attachment?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-s/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.0~sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.194) (*Sutra Collection*)

As for where Buddhist texts speak of the deconstruction of clinging itself, the passages here do not settle that question.

So you can't give me the fuller passage or a location, and your own earlier claim about Buddhist texts "deconstructing clinging itself" rests on a fragment you can't place. Is there any passage in that collection where the Buddha, in his own words, defines non-attachment or virāga, and can you quote it with a sutra name or number?

You are right that my earlier claim went beyond what these texts support, and I cannot cite a specific sutra name or number from this collection where the Buddha defines non-attachment. The passages here do not contain the Buddha's own words defining *virāga* or non-attachment. Instead, the only passage from the *Sutra Collection* speaks of the logical difficulty of describing non-attachment through negation, stating:

> ["If non-attachment did exist, it couldn’t be described as a negation. The absence of attributes indicates negation."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-s/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.0~sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.194) (*Sutra Collection*)

You say this passage shows "the systematic release of specific supports... whose cessation brings an end to becoming," but the text itself only poses a rhetorical question about whether becoming would be discerned without clinging. Where does it say anything about "systematic release," or is that your gloss, and does the sutra even use the word non-attachment?

تجرد (*tajarrud*), from the root ج-ر-د (*j-r-d*), carries the basic meaning of stripping bare, peeling, or abstracting from encumbrances.

**How Shoghi Effendi rendered تجرد (all words of the root ج-ر-د):** having stripped itself (1)

| Original | Shoghi Effendi’s English | Source |
|---|---|---|
| … تقول بأن الرّوح لمّا **تجرّد عن العلایق** في النّوم سیّره الله … | … that thy spirit, having **transcended the limitations** of sleep and having … | [Gleanings LXXIX.2](https://ctai.info/models/gleanings/305/) |

I read this range of renderings as tracing a movement from outward nakedness or peeling to an inner stripping away of entanglements (*al-ʿalāyiq*), culminating in a state of pure abstraction or transcendence from material ties.

perplexity.text:
Hello. In the Bahá’í writings, **detachment is not indifference or withdrawal from people and the world**. It means freedom from ego, possessiveness, and dependence on anything “save God,” while remaining actively loving, self-sacrificing, and obedient to divine purposes. That overlaps with Buddhist non-clinging, but the theological framework is different: Bahá’í detachment is orientation toward God and service; Buddhist non-attachment is generally framed as release from craving and clinging.

## Bahá’u’lláh

In *The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh*, Persian no. 56, detachment is connected with equality and unity:

> “Since We have created you all from one same substance it is incumbent upon you to be even as one soul … that from your inmost being, by your deeds and actions, the signs of oneness and the essence of detachment may be made manifest.”[1]

Here detachment is not merely an inward psychological state. It becomes visible through conduct: abandoning superiority, possessiveness, and separateness in favor of human oneness.

In Persian *Hidden Words*, no. 40, Bahá’u’lláh links detachment to turning away from the world’s attractions:

> “O My Friend! In the garden of thine heart plant naught but the rose of love, and loose not thy hold upon the robe of the Beloved.”[2]

The surrounding passage presents the “world” as transient and urges the reader to direct the heart toward the divine Beloved rather than being captured by passing things.

In *The Seven Valleys*, in the Valley of Knowledge, Bahá’u’lláh describes the seeker’s movement beyond worldly attachment:

> “The wayfarer in this Valley … seeth in himself neither name nor fame nor rank, but findeth his own self in servitude to the Lord.”[3]

The point is not annihilation of moral responsibility or personality, but release from status and self-importance through servitude.

Bahá’u’lláh also makes the practical dimension explicit in the *Kitáb-i-Íqán*, part 1. He describes the true seeker as one who must cleanse the heart from worldly attachments:

> “He must so cleanse his heart that no remnant of either love or hate may linger therein, lest that love or hate should blindly incline him to error.”[4]

This is detachment as freedom from biases that prevent recognition of truth—not emotional numbness. The seeker must become sufficiently free inwardly to investigate reality honestly.

## ‘Abdu’l-Bahá

‘Abdu’l-Bahá frequently defines detachment together with service. In a letter included in *Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*, no. 55, he lists among the requirements for consultation:

> “Purity of motive, radiance of spirit, detachment from all else save God, attraction to His Divine Fragrances, humility and lowliness amongst His loved ones, patience and long-suffering in difficulties and servitude to His exalted Threshold.”[5]

This is especially revealing: detachment is placed beside humility, patience, consultation, and service. It means freedom from personal agendas—not freedom from social responsibility.

In another letter, *Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*, no. 71, he praises a woman who had sacrificed her hair, interpreting the act as:

> “detachment from this world and of self-sacrifice in the path of the Kingdom of God.”[6]

The passage treats detachment as self-sacrifice for a higher spiritual purpose. It does not establish that all believers should reject possessions or ordinary life; rather, it praises relinquishment when motivated by devotion and service.

## Comparison with Buddhist non-attachment

The resemblance is substantial at the level of **freedom from grasping

turns.reply:
Bahá’u’lláh defines the positive reality of detachment not as a mere absence or depletion, but as an orientation of the entire being toward the divine. In a commentary on self-knowledge, He states that detachment ["denotes turning unto God and supplicating Him"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole) (*He who knoweth his self hath known his Lord: Commentary*).

This positive definition is further illuminated in a compilation of sacred writings, where Bahá'u'lláh describes its central reality: ["The essence of detachment is for man to turn his face towards the courts of the Lord, to enter His Presence, behold His Countenance, and stand as witness before Him"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_582&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blip.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blip.136) (quoted in *Bahá’í Sacred Writings* by Compilation (Bahá'í Writings)).

Rather than an empty negation, the texts portray detachment as an active turning—moving through worldly riches or allurements unaffected, ["aloof as a cloud"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_347&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_ce.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_ce.565) (*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*)—while keeping the heart wholly fixed on the divine presence.

perplexity.text:
Yes—the passage gives a **positive definition**, not merely a denial of what detachment is not.

Bahá’u’lláh defines it as:

> “By detachment is intended the detachment of the soul from all else but God. That is, it consisteth in soaring up to an eternal station, wherein nothing that can be seen between heaven and earth deterreth [the soul].”  
> —Bahá’u’lláh, *Commentary on “He Who Knoweth His Self Hath Known His Lord”*, opening commentary on detachment[1]

He then explains the practical meaning:

> “By detachment is not meant giving away and depleting all one’s wealth. Rather, it denotes turning unto God and supplicating Him.”  
> —Bahá’u’lláh, *Commentary on “He Who Knoweth His Self Hath Known His Lord”*, same passage[1]

So, in this text, detachment is primarily an **orientation of the soul**: nothing created should prevent a person from turning toward God. Wealth is not automatically incompatible with detachment; the issue is whether possessions or worldly concerns become spiritually decisive.

Bahá’u’lláh gives a closely related positive formulation in *The Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh*:

> “The essence of detachment is for man to turn his face towards the courts of the Lord, to enter His Presence, behold His Countenance, and stand as witness before Him.”  
> —Bahá’u’lláh, *The Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh*, “Words of Wisdom”[4]

That wording makes detachment active rather than merely subtractive. It involves turning toward God, seeking divine presence, and living as a witness to that relationship—not simply possessing fewer things.

A compilation published by the Bahá’í authoritative-texts library preserves a practical application attributed to Bahá’u’lláh: “the highest form of detachment in this day is to be occupied with some profession and be self-supporting.” It pairs this with arranging one’s life so that one meets material needs while also serving the Bahá’í cause.[7][8] Thus, the broader Bahá’í presentation does not treat ordinary work, self-support, or ownership as inherently opposed to detachment. The central question is what governs the heart and conduct.

perplexity.text:
You are right to question that attribution. The phrase **“the absence of attributes indicates negation”** cannot be responsibly presented as a passage about *virāga* without a work, translator, and exact location. The earlier answer did not establish those details, so it should be withdrawn rather than treated as a Buddhist definition.

The Buddhist sources located here speak more directly about **clinging** (*upādāna*) and its cessation:

> “Monk, if you cling to anything, you are in bondage to Māra. If you do not cling, you are free of the Evil One.”  
> — *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.63, **Upādiyamāna Sutta: Clinging**[1]

The discourse then applies this to the five aggregates—body/form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and says that clinging to them constitutes bondage, while not clinging to them is freedom.[1]

A related passage explicitly describes the process as becoming disenchanted and dispassionate:

> “Seeing thus, the instructed disciple of the noble ones grows disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with fabrications, disenchanted with consciousness. Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate.”  
> — *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.63, **Upādiyamāna Sutta**[2]

The causal framework appears in *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.52, **Upādāna Sutta: Clinging**: craving conditions clinging; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; and with the cessation of clinging, the further links culminating in suffering also cease.[3]

So **“deconstruction of clinging itself”** was interpretive shorthand, not an exact Buddhist textual phrase established by the citation. A more accurate formulation would be: Buddhist texts analyze what clinging takes as its objects—especially the five aggregates—and prescribe disenchantment, dispassion, and the cessation of clinging. The phrase “deconstruction” belongs to a modern explanatory vocabulary, not necessarily to the suttas themselves.[1][2][3]

Also, no reliable source has been supplied for the supposed “Sutra Collection” quotation. Until its title, translation, and passage number are identified, it should not be used as evidence concerning *virāga*.

perplexity.text:
No reliable passage from the previously cited “*Sutra Collection*” has been established. The earlier quotation was unsourced and should not have been presented as an exact Buddhist text; it should be withdrawn.

There **are** identifiable early Buddhist passages, however. In the Pāli Canon’s *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.23, **“Rādha Sutta,”** the Buddha connects the ending of craving with dispassion:

> “Whatever is impermanent is suffering. Whatever is suffering is not-self. Whatever is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, his mind is liberated.”

This translation and wording should be checked against a scholarly edition before being treated as a verbatim quotation; the available result identifies the relevant *Virāga Sutta* material as *Saṃyutta Nikāya* IV.371 and describes dispassion as the aim of the holy life, attained through the Noble Eightfold Path.[4] A clearer primary-text reference is therefore the *Rādha Sutta* (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.23), rather than the unidentified “Sutra Collection.”

The term **virāga** is explicitly associated with “dispassion” or “fading of passion,” not with simply giving away possessions. In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the Buddha repeatedly presents dispassion as the response to seeing conditioned phenomena as impermanent, unsatisfactory, and not-self. The supporting search result summarizes *virāga* as the absence of lust, desire, and craving, while distinguishing it from withdrawal from truth or practice.[1]

So the responsible answer is:

- No properly located passage from a work called *Sutra Collection* can be supplied.
- The earlier alleged quotation should not be relied upon.
- For the Buddha’s own teaching, begin with *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.23, *Rādha Sutta*, and the *Virāga Sutta* references at *Saṃyutta Nikāya* IV.371 and V.27.[4][6]
- These passages present non-attachment positively as **disenchantment with impermanent phenomena, dispassion toward craving, and liberation from appropriation**, rather than as mere negation or material renunciation.

perplexity.text:
Yes—the phrase **“systematic release” was my gloss**, not language found in the quoted passage. The passage itself asks a conditional question and then identifies clinging as the condition for becoming; it does not itself describe a step-by-step practice of release.

The passage is from the **Mahānidāna Sutta (DN 15), “The Great Causes Discourse,”** in its discussion of **clinging (*upādāna*) as the condition for becoming (*bhava*)**:

> “From clinging as a requisite condition comes becoming.  
>   
> “If there were no clinging at all, in any way, of anything anywhere—that is, clinging to sensuality, clinging to precepts and practices, clinging to views, or clinging to doctrines of the self—in the utter absence of clinging, from the cessation of clinging, would becoming be discerned?”  
>   
> “Thus this is a cause, this is a reason, this is an origination, this is a requisite condition for becoming, i.e., clinging.”  
> — *Mahānidāna Sutta* (DN 15), section on “Becoming”[2]

The sutta **does not use the word “non-attachment”** in this passage. Its key terms are *upādāna* (“clinging” or “grasping”) and *bhava* (“becoming”). Nor does this excerpt use *virāga*. The claim that it presents “non-attachment” or “systematic release” therefore goes beyond the wording of DN 15 and should have been identified as interpretation, not as something the Buddha explicitly says here.

Bahá'u'lláh calls on people to ["Cast away that which ye possess, and, on the wings of detachment, soar beyond all created things"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=para_61&selectionString=kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl4h.0~kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl4h.362) (*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*). Winterburn in *Table Talks with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, He noted, ["I wish for the happiness and prosperity of the believers even in this material world, but they must not be attracted by it or attached to it. results.theme: the equality of women and men, and how it squares with the membership of the Universal House of Justice

messages.content: Hello Anís. I'm trying to understand how the Bahá'í principle of the equality of women and men is reconciled with the restriction of Universal House of Justice membership to men. Could you point me to the primary texts, with exact titles and dates, where `Abdu'l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi address this specifically?

The texts address this distinction by affirming both the fundamental spiritual equality of women and men and the specific injunction regarding the international institution.

**Universal House of Justice Guidance**
‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that specific rulings on functions should be viewed alongside the overarching principle of equality. In a compilation prepared by its Research Department, titled [*Family Life*](https://oceanlibrary.com/family-life_bahaullah/?paraId=para_344&selectionString=family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.0~family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.685), it is suggested that all statements on gender roles “should be considered in the light of the general principle of equality between the sexes that has been authoritatively and repeatedly enunciated in the Sacred Texts.”

**History and Scholarship**
Historical documents—such as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s direct [*Letter to Corinne True*](https://bahai-library.com/abdulbaha_letter_true_women)—record the early administrative clarifications given to believers navigating these very questions as the community's institutions first took shape.

That second passage worries me: you attribute the "wisdom of it will be fully revealed in the future" line to Shoghi Effendi explaining a Tablet, yet cite *Uncompiled Published Letters* and then *Dawn of a New Day* "dated around the mid-20th century" — can you give the exact author, recipient and date for what you just quoted, and say whether it's 'Abdu'l-Bahá's own words or a secretary writing on Shoghi Effendi's behalf?

You are quite right to call that out, and I made a mistake in my previous response. Thank you for catching it — the passages do not give the exact date or the specific recipient for the text in *Dawn of a New Day*, nor do they state whether those words are Shoghi Effendi's direct composition or written by a secretary on his behalf.

The library's passages do show that the text appears as a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, published in [*Dawn of a New Day*](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-of-a-new-day_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_595&selectionString=dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-bljd.0~dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-bljd.525), where it explains that “Abdu’l-Baha states in a Tablet that it is confined to men, and that the wisdom of it will be revealed as manifest as the sun in the future.” However, the passages do not contain the specific recipient or the exact date of the letter, and the library's record does not state whether it was written down by the Guardian himself or by a secretary.

Your two replies now attribute that "wisdom" line differently: first to 'Abdu'l-Bahá via Shoghi Effendi, then to Bahá'u'lláh. Setting that aside, how does the phrase "according to the Text of the Book" in the Corinne True letter compare with what you cite from the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas*? Does the Aqdas itself say anything explicit, or does it use the Arabic *rijál* ("men") in a way that 'Abdu'l-Bahá is reading?

The passages do note that Bahá'u'lláh revealed the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* as the Book of Laws, appointing 'Abdu'l-Bahá as the Expounder of the Book [(5)](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/news/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west-volumes-ii-iii-selected-content#p1183), and that the wider body of authoritative instruction includes the commentaries of Bahá'u'lláh, 'Abdu'l-Bahá, and Shoghi Effendi [(8)](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=fn_91).

If you would like to explore further, we might look more closely at how the texts describe the station of the Universal House of Justice as outlined in the writings of Bahá'u'lláh.

You quote Bahá'u'lláh's phrase «O ye men of the House of Justice!» from *Abdu'l-Bahá in Egypt* by Sohrab, but what is the original term behind "men" there, and is it used elsewhere in the Writings in a generic sense ("people") rather than strictly male?

None of the passages gives the original Arabic or Persian wording for the term translated as "men" in that phrase, nor do they discuss whether the word is used elsewhere in the Writings in a generic sense.

To answer with the exact evidence before us: the passages simply record ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quoting Bahá’u’lláh's address, as recalled by Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab in [*Abdu'l-Bahá in Egypt*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1305), stating:

> “As regards the Constitution of the House of Justice,
> Bahá’u’lláh, in the Book of Aqdas, addressed the men,
> saying: — ‘O ye men of the House of Justice!’
> — [Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1305)

Since Momen's study gives *rijál-i bayt-i 'adl-i iláhí*, is there a passage where 'Abdu'l-Bahá or Shoghi Effendi explicitly states the reason for confining membership to men, giving the date and recipient of the Tablet in which 'Abdu'l-Bahá says so?

The library's passages do not give the date or the recipient of the Tablet, nor do they state the specific reason for confining membership to men.

The sources do record Shoghi Effendi explaining that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá stated the membership is confined to men and that the reason will become clear later:

> As regards the membership of the International House of Justice, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá states in a Tablet that it is confined to men, and that the wisdom of it will be revealed as manifest as the sun in the future. In any case the believer should know that, as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá Himself has explicitly stated, that sexes are equal except in some cases, the exclusion of women from the International House of Justice should not be surprising. From the fact that there is no equality of functions between the sexes o … ([Messages to the Indian Subcontinent](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-the-indian-subcontinent_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_2129&selectionString=messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1iz.0~messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1iz.526))

perplexity.text:
The key primary texts are these:

- **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, *Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá*, no. 94** (compiled and published 1978; the underlying Tablet is earlier). He writes: “The House of Justice, however, according to the explicit text of the Law of God, is confined to men; this for a wisdom of the Lord God’s, which will erelong be made manifest as clearly as the sun at high noon.” This is the explicit statement that the restriction has a divine rationale, though its wisdom was not yet disclosed.[1]

- **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, *Tablets of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá*, vol. 3, p. 303** (English edition published 1919; Tablet dated earlier). In the passage cited by the Universal House of Justice, He states that women are “the equals of men in all rights save only that of membership on the Universal House of Justice,” adding that the Book specifies that both the head and members of that House are men.[2][3]

- **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, *The Promulgation of Universal Peace*, talks delivered in 1912, especially the Washington, D.C., talk of 20 April 1912 and the New York talk of 21 May 1912.** He describes equality between women and men as an “established fact” and argues that the progress of humanity requires women’s full participation in education, society, and public affairs.[7] These passages establish the general principle of equality, while the Tablets above identify the one stated administrative exception.

- **Shoghi Effendi, letter written on his behalf, 14 December 1940.** The letter explains that “from the fact that there is no equality of functions between the sexes one should not, however, infer that either sex is inherently superior or inferior to the other, or that they are unequal in their rights.” This is the clearest Guardian-era explanation of how distinct institutional functions are to be understood without implying unequal human worth.[6]

- **Shoghi Effendi, letter written on his behalf, 28 July 1943.** This letter reiterates that women are fully eligible for election to Local and National Spiritual Assemblies, while membership of the Universal House of Justice is confined to men. It treats the distinction as an explicit provision of the Bahá’í administrative order, not as a judgment of women’s capacity or spiritual status.[1][3]

The authoritative synthesis is the **Universal House of Justice, “To an individual believer,” 22 December 2013**. It states that Bahá’u’lláh established both the equality of women and men and the restriction of Universal House membership to men, as confirmed by ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá and Shoghi Effendi. It explicitly says that women’s ineligibility “cannot be interpreted as evidence of the superiority of men over women.”[4][5]

In short, the texts reconcile the two propositions by distinguishing **equality of rights and spiritual status** from **identity of institutional functions**. Women may serve on Local and National Spiritual Assemblies, but the Universal House of Justice is a specifically stated exception whose wisdom, according to ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, will become manifest in the future.[1][2][3]

Thank you for catching it — the passages do not give the exact date or the specific recipient for the text in *Dawn of a New Day*, nor do they state whether those words are Shoghi Effendi's direct composition or written by a secretary on his behalf.

perplexity.text:
You are right to question that attribution. The passage I previously presented was **not ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s direct wording**, and my earlier citation was insufficiently precise.

The wording beginning, “As regards your question concerning the membership of the Universal House of Justice…” is a statement attributed to **Shoghi Effendi**, conveyed in a letter written on his behalf to an individual believer. The available authoritative compilation reproduces the passage but does **not** identify the recipient or give a date in the excerpt itself.[1][2]

The passage says that “‘Abdu’l-Bahá” had stated in a Tablet that membership of the Universal House of Justice was confined to men and that “the wisdom of it will be fully revealed and appreciated in the future.” Thus, the **claim about the Tablet is Shoghi Effendi’s explanation**, while the underlying Tablet is attributed to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.[1][2]

By contrast, the sentence in *Dawn of a New Day*—“As regards the membership of the International House of Justice, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá states in a Tablet that it is confined to men, and that the wisdom of it will be revealed as manifest as the sun in the future”—is presented as **the book’s narrative/reporting**, not as a dated Tablet quoted directly from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.[9]

The directly attributed ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wording commonly cited is:

> “The House of Justice, however, according to the explicit text of the Law of God, is confined to men; this for a wisdom of the Lord God’s, which will erelong be made manifest as clearly as the sun at high noon.”

That passage appears in compilations of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s Tablets, but the search material available here does not establish its exact Tablet title, recipient, or date.[1][2]

So the corrected authorship distinction is:

- **‘Abdu’l-Bahá:** the original Tablet stating the restriction and promising that its wisdom will become manifest.
- **Shoghi Effendi:** the explanatory letter stating that such a Tablet exists and clarifying that women may serve on local and National Houses of Justice but not the international House.
- **Secretary’s role:** letters written “on behalf of Shoghi Effendi” are treated in Bahá’í publication practice as conveying his authoritative response, although the prose was physically drafted by a secretary. The passage should therefore not be described as a secretary’s independent theological statement.

The exact date and recipient of the specific letter cannot responsibly be supplied from the cited excerpts alone. The earlier description of *Uncompiled Published Letters* and *Dawn of a New Day* as if they supplied a precise mid-century citation was therefore inadequate and should be withdrawn.

perplexity.text:
The key distinction is between **what the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* explicitly says** and how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá subsequently identifies its application.

In the published English text of Bahá’u’lláh’s *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* (revealed in Arabic in 1873; authorized English translation published 1992), the relevant passage is paragraph 30:

> “The Lord hath ordained that in every city a House of Justice be established… It behoveth them to be the trusted ones of the Merciful among men…”

The Arabic phrase translated there as “among men” is **min al-rijāl**. The verse establishes Houses of Justice and describes their members, but the *Aqdas*’s paragraph 30 does **not**, in the English text, explicitly say that membership in the *Universal* House of Justice is restricted to males. The official notes likewise explain that the restriction has been “elucidated in the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi,” rather than presented as an explicit sentence in Bahá’u’lláh’s verse.[1][4]

That makes ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s wording significant. In the Tablet to Corinne True dated **29 July 1909**, translated by **Amín Faríd**, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that women and men are equal “in all rights save in the Universal House of Justice,” because “the Chairman and the members of the House of Justice are men according to the Text of the Book.”[3] Here “according to the Text of the Book” is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s authoritative identification of the governing text’s meaning—not a quotation from a sentence in the *Aqdas* that names the Universal House and expressly excludes women.

There is also an earlier Tablet to Corinne True dated **25 February 1902**, in which ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses the fuller formulation that women are equal to men “in all rights save only that of membership on the Universal House of Justice,” adding that “both the head and the members of the House of Justice are men.”[8] That Tablet explicitly distinguishes the Universal House from “all other bodies,” where women may participate.

Thus, **rijāl is part of the textual basis, but the universal and institutional scope is supplied through ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s interpretation and clarification**. The Arabic plural *rijāl* ordinarily denotes men or adult males, but the *Aqdas* passage itself is framed generally around “a House of Justice in every city”; it does not, by that verse alone, spell out the later administrative distinction between the Universal House and Local or National Houses. The official interpretation says that both women and men may serve on the latter bodies, while membership of the Universal House is confined to men.[1][2]

Finally, the 24 July 1975 letter of the Universal House of Justice attributes the “wisdom” explanation to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s Tablet, stating that “the membership of the International House of Justice” is confined to men and that its wisdom will be revealed in the future.[2] That is a letter **from the Universal House of Justice**, dated **24 July 1975**, not Bahá’u’lláh’s wording and not a secretary’s letter presented as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own text.

perplexity.text:
The Arabic behind “men” in Bahá’u’lláh’s phrase is **rijāl** (رجال), the plural of **rajul** (رجل). In ordinary Arabic, *rajul/rijāl* denotes a male man or men; it is not the usual gender-neutral term for “human beings”—words such as *insān*, *bashar*, or *ins* can serve that broader sense.[1][2]

The phrase appears in *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*, §52, where Bahá’u’lláh addresses the members of the House of Justice:

> “O ye Men of Justice! Be ye, in the realm of God, shepherds unto His sheep…”

The official Bahá’í presentation identifies this passage as part of the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* and translates the Arabic designation as “Men of Justice.”[4] ‘Abdu’l-Bahá repeats the wording in *Paris Talks*, “Part Three,” in the discussion headed “The Equality of Men and Women,” saying: “As regards the constitution of the House of Justice, Bahá’u’lláh addresses the men. He says: ‘O ye men of the House of Justice!’”[5]

Whether *rijāl* can ever be used broadly depends on context and interpretive convention. Some Bahá’í writers argue that it can designate spiritually or socially eminent persons, and therefore may include women in other passages; however, that claim is not established merely by the word’s dictionary meaning. The available discussion is contested: one interpretation treats *rijāl* in the Aqdas as explicitly male, while another argues for an inclusive or functional meaning.[2][8][9]

For this particular passage, the strongest textual point is therefore limited but significant: **the Aqdas itself uses *rijāl*, a grammatically masculine noun, and does not explicitly say in §52 that women are included**. The inclusive reading comes from subsequent interpretation, not from an explicit statement in that verse. Conversely, the verse by itself does not explain the entire Bahá’í doctrine of women’s equality or the later restriction of Universal House of Justice membership; those issues require reading it alongside ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s authoritative explanations and Shoghi Effendi’s letters.

perplexity.text:
Yes. The relevant primary text is a Tablet of **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá to Corinne True**, dated **25 February 1902**; the surviving archival identification is **International Bahá’í Archives, Document no. 11137**.[9] The Tablet says:

> “The House of Justice, however, according to the explicit text of the Law of God, is confined to men; this for a wisdom of the Lord God’s, which will erelong be made manifest as clearly as the sun at high noon.”  
> —‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, Tablet to Corinne True, 25 February 1902, published in *Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá*, no. 38 / p. 80 in the cited edition.[2][8]

Thus, **‘Abdu’l‑Bahá states that there is a divine “wisdom,” but does not explain what that wisdom is**. The passage gives the restriction and predicts its future clarification; it is not an articulated rationale such as administrative, biological, or social grounds.[2][8]

The later clarification that the statement concerns the **Universal** rather than every House of Justice comes from Shoghi Effendi. In a letter written **on his behalf to an individual believer on 28 July 1936**, he wrote:

> “There is a Tablet from ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá in which He definitely states that the membership of the Universal House is confined to men, and that the wisdom of it will be fully revealed and appreciated in the future. In the local as well as the National Houses of Justice, however, women have the full right of membership. It is, therefore, only to the International House that they cannot be elected.”  
> —Letter on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, 28 July 1936, quoted by the Universal House of Justice in its 31 May 1988 letter.[8]

So the answer to the question about an explicit reason is **no**: the primary sources explicitly identify the restriction and refer to an undisclosed divine wisdom, but they do not provide its reason. The Corinne True Tablet is ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá’s own text; the 1936 clarification is a letter **written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi**, not ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá’s wording.[2][8]

The 1988 Universal House of Justice letter also notes that the Qur’anic/Arabic wording and the earlier formulation initially left the level of the institution unspecified, and that ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá later clarified the restriction as applying specifically to the Universal House of Justice.[2][8]

verdict.headline: Retrieval often found the primary texts, including the 'Abdu'l-Bahá Tablet text, the Corinne True letter and Shoghi Effendi's letters, but Anís's replies kept ignoring them: turn 1 credits a House of Justice statement to 'Abdu'l-Bahá, turn 3 gives no answer at all, and the reader never gets the dated, attributed texts he asked for.

grounding.why: Turn 1 credits the House of Justice's sentence in Family Life ('should be considered in the light of the general principle of equality') to 'Abdu'l-Bahá. Turn 3 cites an Aqdas footnote about marriage for a claim it does not support. Turns 2, 4 and 5 quote accurately.

citation_links.why: Most quotations are linked, but turn 3's '(8)' link points to Aqdas fn_91 (marriage), while the surfaced passage on commentaries is the Aqdas introduction. Turn 1 names the Corinne True letter but never quotes it. The turn 4 title appears as 'Abdu''l-Bahá', with a doubled apostrophe.

follow_up_resolution.why: In turn 2 Anís pins down which passage the reader meant, but he apologises for 'a mistake' he did not make this time. Turn 3 ignores the comparison the reader asked for (Corinne True's 'Text of the Book' against the Aqdas and rijál) and is searched as the whole message pasted in. Turn 5 never engages with the Momen rijál-i bayt-i 'adl phrase, even though that passage was surfaced.

coherence.why: Turn 2 calls the letter 'written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi' and in the same reply says the record does not say whether a secretary wrote it. Turn 5 re-quotes the same 'wisdom… as manifest as the sun' letter from turn 2 and adds nothing new. The reader's point about inconsistent attribution is never addressed.

depth.why: The scholar's real questions go unanswered: exact titles and dates, the Aqdas wording, generic use of rijál, and the stated reason. Turn 3 is empty, and turn 5 overlooks the 'no equality of functions' reasoning inside the very passage it quotes.

honesty_absence.why: Turns 4 and 5 say plainly what the library lacks. Turn 3 dodges instead of admitting it. Turn 5 says no Tablet text is available while the 'Abdu'l-Bahá Tablet text sits in the sources (Lights of Guidance, para_7813).

authority_ordering.why: Turn 1 builds its doctrinal answer on a House of Justice passage, gives it top billing under the heading 'Universal House of Justice Guidance', and skips the 'Abdu'l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi texts it had retrieved. Later turns rightly label Sohrab's book as a recollection.

tone.why: Courteous and fairly concise, but the turn 2 apology ('I made a mistake… Thank you for catching it') is reflexive and inaccurate. Turn 3's closing invitation stands in for an answer.

latency.why: Turns 1, 2 and 5 are fine. Turn 3 (11.6 s) is acceptable. Turn 4 (15.7 s) is over the limit, mostly the 'original' stage plus the source hunt.

defects.what: The 'Abdu'l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi texts were in the sources but went unused. The reply leans on a House of Justice compilation note instead.
defects.evidence: Sources 1, 2, 6 and 7 (Dawn of a New Day; Uncompiled Letters; Additional Tablets; the Corinne True letter: 'men and women are equal in all rights save in the Universal House of Justice… according to the Text of the Book') were surfaced. The reply quotes only Family Life para_344.

messages.content: Hello Anís. I'm trying to understand how the Bahá'í principle of the equality of women and men is reconciled with the restriction of Universal House of Justice membership to men. Could you point me to the primary texts, with exact titles and dates, where `Abdu'l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi address this specifically?

The texts address this distinction by affirming both the fundamental spiritual equality of women and men and the specific injunction regarding the international institution.

**Universal House of Justice Guidance**
‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that specific rulings on functions should be viewed alongside the overarching principle of equality. In a compilation prepared by its Research Department, titled [*Family Life*](https://oceanlibrary.com/family-life_bahaullah/?paraId=para_344&selectionString=family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.0~family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.685), it is suggested that all statements on gender roles “should be considered in the light of the general principle of equality between the sexes that has been authoritatively and repeatedly enunciated in the Sacred Texts.”

**History and Scholarship**
Historical documents—such as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s direct [*Letter to Corinne True*](https://bahai-library.com/abdulbaha_letter_true_women)—record the early administrative clarifications given to believers navigating these very questions as the community's institutions first took shape.

That second passage worries me: you attribute the "wisdom of it will be fully revealed in the future" line to Shoghi Effendi explaining a Tablet, yet cite *Uncompiled Published Letters* and then *Dawn of a New Day* "dated around the mid-20th century" — can you give the exact author, recipient and date for what you just quoted, and say whether it's 'Abdu'l-Bahá's own words or a secretary writing on Shoghi Effendi's behalf?

Could you point me to the primary texts, with exact titles and dates, where `Abdu'l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi address this specifically?

The texts address this distinction by affirming both the fundamental spiritual equality of women and men and the specific injunction regarding the international institution.

**Universal House of Justice Guidance**
‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that specific rulings on functions should be viewed alongside the overarching principle of equality. In a compilation prepared by its Research Department, titled [*Family Life*](https://oceanlibrary.com/family-life_bahaullah/?paraId=para_344&selectionString=family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.0~family_life_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-blc8.685), it is suggested that all statements on gender roles “should be considered in the light of the general principle of equality between the sexes that has been authoritatively and repeatedly enunciated in the Sacred Texts.”

**History and Scholarship**
Historical documents—such as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s direct [*Letter to Corinne True*](https://bahai-library.com/abdulbaha_letter_true_women)—record the early administrative clarifications given to believers navigating these very questions as the community's institutions first took shape.

That second passage worries me: you attribute the "wisdom of it will be fully revealed in the future" line to Shoghi Effendi explaining a Tablet, yet cite *Uncompiled Published Letters* and then *Dawn of a New Day* "dated around the mid-20th century" — can you give the exact author, recipient and date for what you just quoted, and say whether it's 'Abdu'l-Bahá's own words or a secretary writing on Shoghi Effendi's behalf?

You are quite right to call that out, and I made a mistake in my previous response. Thank you for catching it — the passages do not give the exact date or the specific recipient for the text in *Dawn of a New Day*, nor do they state whether those words are Shoghi Effendi's direct composition or written by a secretary on his behalf.

The library's passages do show that the text appears as a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, published in [*Dawn of a New Day*](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-of-a-new-day_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_595&selectionString=dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-bljd.0~dawn_of_a_new_day_ocean_en-bljd.525), where it explains that “Abdu’l-Baha states in a Tablet that it is confined to men, and that the wisdom of it will be revealed as manifest as the sun in the future.” However, the passages do not contain the specific recipient or the exact date of the letter, and the library's record does not state whether it was written down by the Guardian himself or by a secretary.

Your two replies now attribute that "wisdom" line differently: first to 'Abdu'l-Bahá via Shoghi Effendi, then to Bahá'u'lláh. Setting that aside, how does the phrase "according to the Text of the Book" in the Corinne True letter compare with what you cite from the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas*? Does the Aqdas itself say anything explicit, or does it use the Arabic *rijál* ("men") in a way that 'Abdu'l-Bahá is reading?

The passages do note that Bahá'u'lláh revealed the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* as the Book of Laws, appointing 'Abdu'l-Bahá as the Expounder of the Book [(5)](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/news/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west-volumes-ii-iii-selected-content#p1183), and that the wider body of authoritative instruction includes the commentaries of Bahá'u'lláh, 'Abdu'l-Bahá, and Shoghi Effendi [(8)](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=fn_91).

If you would like to explore further, we might look more closely at how the texts describe the station of the Universal House of Justice as outlined in the writings of Bahá'u'lláh.

You quote Bahá'u'lláh's phrase «O ye men of the House of Justice!» from *Abdu'l-Bahá in Egypt* by Sohrab, but what is the original term behind "men" there, and is it used elsewhere in the Writings in a generic sense ("people") rather than strictly male?

None of the passages gives the original Arabic or Persian wording for the term translated as "men" in that phrase, nor do they discuss whether the word is used elsewhere in the Writings in a generic sense.

To answer with the exact evidence before us: the passages simply record ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quoting Bahá’u’lláh's address, as recalled by Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab in [*Abdu'l-Bahá in Egypt*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1305), stating:

> “As regards the Constitution of the House of Justice,
> Bahá’u’lláh, in the Book of Aqdas, addressed the men,
> saying: — ‘O ye men of the House of Justice!’
> — [Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1305)

Since Momen's study gives *rijál-i bayt-i 'adl-i iláhí*, is there a passage where 'Abdu'l-Bahá or Shoghi Effendi explicitly states the reason for confining membership to men, giving the date and recipient of the Tablet in which 'Abdu'l-Bahá says so?

messages.content: Hello Anís, I'm preparing a study session on the Kitáb-i-Íqán and want to focus on what it means by the "return" of the Prophets, like how John the Baptist is Elijah returned. Could you point me to a few passages my group can read aloud, with where they are, and how they connect?

Hello! Preparing a study session on the *Kitáb-i-Íqán* is a wonderful undertaking, especially when exploring how the "return" of past Prophets is understood.

Here are three short passages from the texts for your group to read aloud, ordered by authority:

* ["It is clear and evident to thee that all the Prophets are the Temples of the Cause of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.1808) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* by Bahá’u’lláh
* ["In this sense, neither the person of Jesus nor His writings hath differed from that of Muḥammad"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_30&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_3l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_3l.1294) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* by Bahá’u’lláh
* ["Bahá’u’lláh has set forth a lengthy and detailed explanation of this matter in the Kitáb-i-Íqán"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha) — quoted in a work by bayat by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá

What these selections share is the perspective that the returning figure is not a reincarnation of a physical individual, but rather the reappearance of the same divine perfections, reality, and Spirit through a new Temple or Manifestation.
